abstract: Animals use social information to make decisions, yet how such processes influence predictions in reproductive timing and population adaptation under environmental change remains unclear. While social information can improve decision accuracy through information pooling, spatiotemporal heterogeneity in conditions and patterns of environmental changes creates noise that potentially limits the value of social information use among breeding individuals. Here, we established an evolutionary individual-based model to examine how social and private sensing interact to shape breeding phenology in species distributed across territories with peaked resources and facing annual fluctuations and rapid climate change. We show that when individuals incorporate social information from neighbours, behavioural responses become increasingly synchronised through positive feedback in decision-making. This emergent synchrony helps populations to adapt faster and can increase reproductive output under stable environmental conditions relative to relying only on private information. However, under directional climate change, the same mechanism reduces population responsiveness by constraining variation in individual responses, leading to systematic lag in tracking shifting environmental optima and reduced population reproductive output. Our results demonstrate that social information use can produce a general trade-off at the population level between synchronisation and adaptive flexibility across environmental contexts. Social interaction enhances population performance when environments are either consistent or changing drastically across both spatial and temporal scales. Rather than uniformly improving performance, social interaction may create conditions under which collective behaviour becomes maladaptive when environments change rapidly.
